newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO names U.S. Cuba law panel, EU seeks deal.
newsitem.headline: WTO names U.S. Cuba law panel, EU seeks deal.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Thursday named three international experts to adjudicate in the EU-US row over investment in Cuba but Brussels insisted it still wanted to find a solution in direct talks with Washington.

WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero appointed the three to a dispute panel after a meeting with the top trade diplomats from the two powers in Geneva made clear they were still far apart on the potentially explosive issue.

But WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell said the move -- automatic once the EU had said it wanted to pursue a case through the body's dispute settlement procedure -- "in no way precludes negotiations between the parties in any forum they choose."
If this took place outside the trade body, said Rockwell, "that's fine by us."

And EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said it remained Brussels' aim "to achieve a negotiated settlement" through bilateral contacts -- which he added had made "good progress" in recent weeks but not enough to halt the WTO action.

The three panelists, who have six months to produce a clearly difficult finding, include Arthur Dunkel, Swiss former head of the old General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) -- which was replaced by the more powerful WTO in 1995.

The other two are Tommy Koh, Singapore's ambassador-at-large and an experienced international diplomat, and Edward Woodfield, New Zealand's top trade negotiator throughout the 1980s and currently an independent consultant.

At the heart of the dispute is the U.S. Helms-Burton law which aims to stop non-American firms investing in Cuba by leaving them open to prosecution in U.S. courts and by refusing visas to their executives to visit the United States.

The panel's task will be complicated by the emotional, and electoral, dimension of U.S. relations with Cuba and President Fidel Castro, and the power of Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman Jessie Helms, co-author of the law.

The EU -- backed by Canada, Mexico and almost all other countries in the 130-member WTO -- argues Helms-Burton violates open trade rules, partly designed by the United States itself, by extending U.S. judicial reach outside national territory.

In its submission to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB), which last November approved creation of a panel, Brussels says aspects of the law run against agreed rules on both trade in goods and on trade in services.

But the United States counters that the law, signed by President Bill Clinton after Cuban jets shot down two small planes flown by anti-communist exiles near the island a year ago, is a matter of "national security" and outside the WTO purview.

A scarcely-tested clause in the GATT, which is also the underlying rule-book for the WTO, appears to allow a member country to suspend compliance with the entire agreement if it determines that its national security is at stake.
U.S. officials argue that only the government concerned can judge whether it faces a security threat.
But the EU insists that if action is taken affecting trade between third countries, then a WTO panel must decide if recourse to the "national security" clause is justified.

Many diplomats and trade analysts who agree with the EU nevertheless fear that the panel process -- which can be followed by an appeals prodecure which could take a further three months -- could be damaging for the WTO.

Echoing warnings from Clinton administration officials, they say a finding that went against the United States would be bound to strengthen anti-free trade hardliners in Congress who say membership of the WTO is a threat to U.S. sovereignty.
